specStatements.text: In some chemical reactions, the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. Such reactions are called reversible reactions and are represented:
A +B ⇌C + D
The direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions.
For example:
If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction. The same amount of energy is transferred in each case. For example:
When a reversible reaction occurs in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.
If a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change.
The effects of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium can be predicted using Le Chatelier’s Principle.
Students should be able to make qualitative predictions about the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium when given appropriate information.

If the concentration of one of the reactants or products is changed, the system is no longer at equilibrium and the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again.
If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.
If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.
Students should be able to interpret appropriate given data to predict the effect of a change in concentration of a reactant or product on given reactions at equilibrium.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is increased:
the relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction
the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an exothermic reaction.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is decreased:
the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction
the relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an exothermic reaction.
Students should be able to interpret appropriate given data to predict the effect of a change in temperature on given reactions at equilibrium.
For gaseous reactions at equilibrium:
an increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction
a decrease in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the larger number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.
Students should be able to interpret appropriate given data to predict the effect of pressure changes on given reactions at equilibrium.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to make qualitative predictions about the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium when given appropriate information.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every prediction asked for here is qualitative and every question supplies the information it needs. Students are asked only which way the position of equilibrium shifts and whether the amount of a named substance rises, falls or is unchanged. Whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and the symbol equation to count molecules from, are always given in the stem rather than assumed. Nothing asks for an equilibrium constant, for a numerical yield to be calculated, or for the magnitude of a shift, and no item requires knowledge of a named industrial process, which is treated elsewhere in the specification.

The pressure rule is applied only to reactions in which every substance is a gas, and each such question says so. Molecules are counted only from the symbol equation given, as the specification requires. No item introduces equilibria involving solids or liquids alongside gases, and none asks students to decide which species should be counted in a mixed-state equilibrium, which the specification does not cover at this level.

concepts.definition: A reaction in which the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. The change is not a dead end: once some product has formed, that product is able to turn back into the starting substances.

The double half-arrow used to represent a reversible reaction, as in A + B ⇌ C + D. It shows that A and B can react to give C and D, and that C and D can react to give A and B. A single arrow → would mean only one of those two changes is possible.

In A + B ⇌ C + D the forward reaction is A + B → C + D, read left to right, and the reverse reaction is C + D → A + B, read right to left. Which substances count as 'reactants' therefore depends on which of the two reactions is being described.

concepts.term: Changing the direction by changing the conditions
concepts.definition: The direction of a reversible reaction can be changed by changing the conditions. The same set of substances can be made to go one way under one set of conditions, such as heating, and the other way under another, such as cooling.

concepts.term: Ammonium chloride: a worked example of changing direction
concepts.definition: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride, or NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. Heating the white solid drives the forward reaction and produces the two gases; where the gases meet a cooler surface the reverse reaction happens and white solid ammonium chloride forms again.

concepts.term: Energy transfer in the two directions
concepts.definition: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each case. If the forward reaction transfers a given quantity of energy to the surroundings, the reverse reaction takes exactly that quantity in.

concepts.term: Hydrated and anhydrous copper sulfate: a worked example of energy transfer
concepts.definition: hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water, or CuSO4.5H2O ⇌ CuSO4 + 5H2O. Heating the blue hydrated solid to drive off water is endothermic and leaves a white solid; adding water to the white anhydrous solid is exothermic, the mixture warms up and the blue colour returns.

Apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products. Equilibrium can only be reached in such apparatus, because a substance that escapes is no longer available to take part in the reverse reaction.

The state reached, in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. Because the two rates are equal, the amounts of the substances present stop changing.
Equilibrium is dynamic, not static. Both reactions are still occurring at equilibrium; they are simply occurring at exactly the same rate as each other, so no change can be observed from outside.

The relative amounts of all the reactants and products present at equilibrium. These relative amounts depend on the conditions of the reaction, so the same reaction can settle with mostly products under one set of conditions and mostly reactants under another.

If a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, the system responds to counteract the change. The response opposes the change made; it reduces its effect but does not undo it entirely.

The principle that the effects of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium can be predicted from the idea that the system responds to counteract the change made. It is used to predict the direction in which the position of equilibrium moves, not how quickly equilibrium is reached.

Using given information about a reaction, such as its equation and whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, to say which way the position of equilibrium moves and whether the amount of a named substance rises or falls. Only this qualitative judgement is required.

concepts.term: Effect of a change in concentration
concepts.definition: If the concentration of one of the reactants or products is changed, the system is no longer at equilibrium, and the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again. A change made to one substance therefore affects every substance in the equilibrium.

concepts.term: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
concepts.definition: If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again. The system counteracts the extra reactant by using some of it up.

concepts.term: Decreasing the concentration of a product
concepts.definition: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again. Removing a product does not stop the reaction; it causes more of the product to be made.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is increased, the relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction and decreases for an exothermic reaction.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is decreased, the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction and increases for an exothermic reaction.

concepts.term: Counting molecules from the symbol equation
concepts.definition: For gaseous reactions, the number of molecules on each side is read from the balanced symbol equation, using the big numbers in front of the formulae. In N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 there are four molecules on the left and two on the right.

For gaseous reactions at equilibrium, an increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.

For gaseous reactions at equilibrium, a decrease in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the larger number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.

concepts.term: Equal numbers of molecules on each side
concepts.definition: If the symbol equation shows the same number of gas molecules on both sides, as in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, a change in pressure gives no side for the equilibrium to shift towards, so the relative amounts at equilibrium are unaffected by pressure.

Data such as the percentage yield of a product measured at different temperatures, pressures or concentrations can be read backwards: the direction in which the yield moves tells you which way the position of equilibrium has shifted, and therefore what the reaction must be like.

misconceptions.question: A reversible reaction is written A + B ⇌ C + D. Does it go forwards first and then backwards?
misconceptions.correct: Neither direction has to wait for the other. As soon as any C and D exist they can react to give A and B back.
misconceptions.misconception: A reversible reaction runs all the way forwards until the reactants are used up, and only then turns round and runs all the way back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday reversible things are sequential - a swing goes out and then comes back, a video plays and then rewinds - so students import that one-then-the-other picture into chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. That is possible from the moment any product exists, so both changes can be happening in the same mixture at the same time.

misconceptions.question: In A + B ⇌ C + D, can C and D ever be called reactants?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. In the reverse reaction C and D are the reactants and A and B are the products.
misconceptions.misconception: The left-hand side of an equation is always the reactants and the right-hand side is always the products, so C and D can only ever be products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught to read equations left to right from the very beginning, and a reversible reaction is the first time that rule stops being the whole story.
misconceptions.correction: The ⇌ symbol shows two reactions. Read left to right, A and B are the reactants; read right to left, C and D are the reactants. Which substances are the reactants depends on which of the two reactions you mean.

misconceptions.question: A reaction has gone in the forward direction. Can it be made to go the other way?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a reaction has happened it is done; you cannot make it run the other way, because the products are new substances now.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every reaction met before this point is treated as one-way, and irreversible examples such as burning are used so often that irreversibility feels like a rule about all reactions.
misconceptions.correction: For a reversible reaction the direction is not fixed by the reaction, it is fixed by the conditions. Changing the conditions, for example heating instead of cooling, changes which direction the reaction goes in.

misconceptions.question: Ammonium chloride is heated and a white solid re-forms further up the tube. What has happened?
misconceptions.correct: The solid decomposed into ammonia and hydrogen chloride, and those two gases reacted again where it was cooler.
misconceptions.misconception: The ammonium chloride simply turned into a gas and then back into a solid; it is a physical change, like ice melting and freezing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The observation - solid disappears at the hot end, identical solid appears at the cool end - looks exactly like sublimation, and no new substance is visible in between.
misconceptions.correction: The change is chemical: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Heating breaks it into two different gases, and the reverse reaction between those gases makes ammonium chloride again on the cool glass.

misconceptions.question: A forward reaction transfers 176 kJ to the surroundings. How much does the reverse reaction take in?
misconceptions.correct: Exactly 176 kJ. The same amount of energy is transferred in each case.
misconceptions.misconception: The reverse reaction takes in less than the forward reaction gave out, because some energy is always lost on the way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that energy is wasted in machines and in energy transfer chains, and carry that idea across to the energy change of a reaction, which is a fixed quantity.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise here: if a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each case.

misconceptions.question: The forward reaction is exothermic. What is the reverse reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Endothermic. The two directions are always opposite in this respect.
misconceptions.misconception: The reverse reaction is exothermic too, because a reaction always gives out energy when it happens.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most reactions students meet and remember - burning, neutralisation, metal with acid - are exothermic, so 'reactions give out heat' becomes a general rule in their minds.
misconceptions.correction: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction. Making the bonds that the forward reaction broke must take in the energy that breaking them released.

misconceptions.question: Water is added to white anhydrous copper sulfate. Does the mixture warm up or cool down?
misconceptions.correct: It warms up. The reaction forming hydrated copper sulfate is exothermic.
misconceptions.misconception: It must cool down, because you had to heat the blue solid to get the white one, so energy has to be put in to change it back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The heating step is the memorable, visible one in the lesson, and students assume that anything you do to this substance needs energy supplying.
misconceptions.correction: Heating hydrated copper sulfate is the endothermic direction. The opposite direction, adding water back, must therefore be exothermic, and it transfers the same amount of energy out again.

misconceptions.question: A reaction in a sealed flask has reached equilibrium. What are the two reactions doing?
misconceptions.correct: Both are still occurring, at exactly the same rate as each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Both reactions have stopped, because nothing in the flask is changing any more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Nothing is changing' is read as 'nothing is happening'. Students have no way of seeing particles reacting, so a constant appearance is taken to mean a finished reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. They are both still going; each one replaces exactly what the other removes, so no change can be observed.

misconceptions.question: At equilibrium, are the amounts of reactants and products equal?
misconceptions.correct: Not usually. Equal rates are required, not equal amounts.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium means the reactants and the products are present in equal amounts - that is what the word balance means.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'equilibrium' and 'balance' is equality of the two sides, and diagrams of see-saws and balances are used to introduce the word.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines equilibrium by the rates: it is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. The relative amounts of reactants and products depend on the conditions and are usually not equal.

misconceptions.question: Can a reversible reaction reach equilibrium in an open beaker?
misconceptions.correct: No. Equilibrium needs apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium will be reached in any container as long as you wait long enough; the lid only matters for safety.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of equilibrium as something that happens with time rather than something that depends on nothing being lost from the mixture.
misconceptions.correction: If a product escapes it cannot take part in the reverse reaction, so the reverse reaction can never match the forward one and the forward reaction simply continues. The specification requires apparatus which prevents escape.

misconceptions.question: What fixes the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: The conditions of the reaction, such as temperature, pressure and concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: The balanced symbol equation fixes them - the big numbers tell you the proportions you end up with at equilibrium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balanced equations are used throughout chemistry to work out amounts, so students expect them to give the equilibrium amounts too.
misconceptions.correction: The equation gives the ratio in which substances react, not the amounts left at equilibrium. The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.

misconceptions.question: A condition is changed and the system responds. Does it end up exactly where it started?
misconceptions.correct: No. It counteracts the change, reducing its effect, but does not cancel it out.
misconceptions.misconception: The system undoes the change completely and goes back to exactly the same position of equilibrium it had before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'counteract' is heard as 'cancel', and Le Chatelier's Principle is often summarised in class as the system 'opposing' the change, which sounds total.
misconceptions.correction: The system responds to counteract the change, which means it shifts in the direction that opposes it. If it undid the change entirely, changing the conditions could never change the yield, and it clearly does.

misconceptions.question: What does Le Chatelier’s Principle let you predict?
misconceptions.correct: The direction in which the position of equilibrium shifts when a condition is changed.
misconceptions.misconception: It tells you how much faster the reaction goes and how quickly equilibrium will be reached.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equilibrium is taught straight after rates of reaction, so temperature, pressure and concentration are already firmly attached in students' minds to speed rather than to yield.
misconceptions.correction: Le Chatelier's Principle is about the position of equilibrium, that is, the relative amounts present once equilibrium is reached again. It says nothing about how long that takes.

misconceptions.question: More of a reactant is added to a system at equilibrium. Which way does the position of equilibrium shift?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the products. More products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.
misconceptions.misconception: Towards the reactants, because that is the side you have just added to, so that side is now the bigger one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Shifts towards' is misread as 'moves to where the extra material is', instead of as the direction in which the system reacts to remove it.
misconceptions.correction: The system responds to counteract the change. The way to counteract extra reactant is to use some of it up, so the forward reaction runs further and more products are formed.

misconceptions.question: A product is continuously removed from an equilibrium mixture. What happens to the reaction?
misconceptions.correct: More reactants react, so more of that product is formed until equilibrium is reached again.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction stops or goes backwards, because you have taken away the substance the system needs to stay in balance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Removing something feels like taking away a resource, and students think of the products as being needed to keep the reverse reaction, and therefore the equilibrium, going.
misconceptions.correction: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again. Removing a product is a way of making more product form, not of stopping the reaction.

misconceptions.question: Extra A is added to A + B ⇌ C + D. Which concentrations change?
misconceptions.correct: All of them. Every concentration changes until equilibrium is reached again.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the concentration of A changes, because A is the only substance that was added to the flask.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the four substances as separate stores rather than as one linked system, so a change made to one is expected to stay with that one.
misconceptions.correction: The system is no longer at equilibrium, so both reactions adjust: the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again. A falls back somewhat, B falls, C and D rise.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the temperature always increase the amount of product at equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: No. It increases the amount of products only if the forward reaction is endothermic.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating always gives you more product, because reactions go faster and get further when they are hot.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In rates work, raising the temperature always speeds a reaction up, and speed is easily confused with how far a reaction goes.
misconceptions.correction: Raising the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction, but decreases it for an exothermic one. Whether the yield rises or falls depends on the energy change of the forward reaction.

misconceptions.question: Which direction does heating a system at equilibrium favour?
misconceptions.correct: The endothermic direction, because that direction takes energy in and so counteracts the heating.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating favours the exothermic direction and cooling favours the endothermic direction, because heat goes with the exothermic reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link the word 'heating' to the word 'exothermic' because both involve heat, and pair the terms rather than thinking about which change opposes what was done.
misconceptions.correction: The system counteracts the change. Raising the temperature is counteracted by the direction that takes energy in, the endothermic one; lowering it is counteracted by the direction that gives energy out, the exothermic one.

misconceptions.question: The pressure on a gaseous equilibrium is increased. Which side does it shift towards?
misconceptions.correct: The side with the smaller number of molecules shown by the symbol equation.
misconceptions.misconception: The side with more molecules, because raising the pressure squeezes more gas molecules into the container.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is associated with 'more gas', so students expect a pressure rise to push the system towards whichever side has more gas molecules on it.
misconceptions.correction: An increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules. Fewer gas molecules in the same space is what reduces, and so counteracts, the raised pressure.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the pressure always increase the yield of the product of a gaseous reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. It only does so if the product side has the smaller number of molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Higher pressure always forces the reaction on and gives a better yield of product, whatever the equation shows.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Industrial chemistry is usually met through the Haber process, where high pressure does raise the yield, and that single case is generalised into a rule.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of the shift is decided by the numbers of molecules in the symbol equation. If the product side has more molecules the yield falls, and if both sides have the same number the pressure makes no difference.

misconceptions.question: How do you decide which side of a gaseous equation has fewer molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Count the molecules, using the big numbers in front of the formulae in the balanced equation.
misconceptions.misconception: Count the atoms on each side; the side with fewer atoms is the side the equilibrium shifts to at high pressure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing equations trains students to count atoms, and that habit is applied here even though a balanced equation always has equal numbers of atoms on both sides.
misconceptions.correction: A balanced equation has the same number of atoms on both sides by definition, so counting atoms can never distinguish them. Pressure depends on the number of molecules: in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 that is four on the left and two on the right.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes what makes a reaction a reversible reaction?

options.text: The products of the reaction can react to make the original reactants
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification: in some chemical reactions the products can react to produce the original reactants.

options.text: The reaction runs fully forwards and then runs fully backwards again
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture reversibility as one complete change followed by another, like a video rewinding.

options.text: The reaction ends with equal amounts of reactants and products
options.rationale: Comes from reading 'reversible' as meaning the two sides must end up balanced against each other.

options.text: The reaction can be made to go faster or slower by adding a catalyst
options.rationale: Picked by students who confuse a reaction that can change direction with one whose rate can be changed.

mcqs.stem: A reversible reaction is represented as A + B ⇌ C + D. What does this representation tell you about C and D?

options.text: They are products of the equation and so can never act as reactants
options.rationale: Follows the habit of reading every equation left to right, with the right-hand side as a dead end.

options.text: They can react together to form A and B again under the right conditions
options.rationale: The ⇌ symbol shows that the change works in both directions, so C and D can react to give the original reactants.

options.text: They are formed completely first and then break down to give A and B
options.rationale: The sequential picture of a reversible reaction: all the way one way, then all the way back.

options.text: They must always be present in the same amounts as A and B are
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the ⇌ symbol means the two sides are equal in amount.

mcqs.stem: A reversible reaction is currently going in the forward direction. How could it be made to go in the reverse direction?

options.text: It cannot be changed once the forward reaction has already started off
options.rationale: Comes from treating all reactions as one-way, as burning and other irreversible examples are.

options.text: By waiting, because a reversible reaction turns round by itself at the end
options.rationale: Assumes the reverse change happens automatically once the forward one has finished.

options.text: By changing the conditions, for example by cooling it instead of heating
options.rationale: The specification states that the direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions.

options.text: By adding a catalyst, which drives the reaction the opposite way round
options.rationale: Confuses changing the rate of a reaction with changing the direction it goes in.

mcqs.stem: Ammonium chloride is heated at the bottom of a test tube: NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. A white solid forms on the cool upper part of the tube. Why?

options.text: The solid melted, travelled up the tube as a vapour and then set again
options.rationale: The observation looks like sublimation, so the chemical decomposition is missed entirely.

options.text: The forward reaction has now finished, so the reverse reaction can begin
options.rationale: Uses the one-then-the-other picture instead of different conditions in different parts of the tube.

options.text: Some ammonium chloride powder was carried up the tube by the hot gases
options.rationale: A physical explanation that fits the appearance of the solid but ignores the equation given.

options.text: The cooler conditions let ammonia and hydrogen chloride react together again
options.rationale: The reverse reaction is favoured by the cooler conditions higher up the tube, re-forming solid ammonium chloride.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. What can be said about the reverse reaction?

options.text: It is endothermic, and transfers the same amount of energy
options.rationale: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the other, with the same energy transfer.

options.text: It is exothermic too, because reactions release energy
options.rationale: Rests on the belief that all reactions give out energy, formed from exothermic examples.

options.text: It is endothermic, but transfers less energy than the forward
options.rationale: Imports the idea of wasted energy from energy transfer chains into the energy change of a reaction.

options.text: It is exothermic, unless the conditions are changed first
options.rationale: Mixes up the energy change of the reverse reaction with the conditions needed to bring it about.

mcqs.stem: In a reversible reaction the forward reaction transfers 176 kJ of energy to the surroundings. What happens in the reverse reaction?

options.text: Less than 176 kJ is taken in from them
options.rationale: Assumes some energy is lost, so less can be taken back in.

options.text: 176 kJ is taken in from the surroundings
options.rationale: The same amount of energy is transferred in each case, but in the opposite direction.

options.text: 176 kJ is given out to the surroundings
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect energy to be released whichever way the reaction goes.

options.text: Twice as much, 352 kJ, is taken in
options.rationale: A doubling error from thinking the reverse reaction must supply the forward one as well.

mcqs.stem: Blue hydrated copper sulfate is heated and turns into white anhydrous copper sulfate and water. This change is endothermic. What happens when water is added to the white solid?

options.text: It turns blue and the mixture cools down, as energy is taken in
options.rationale: Assumes that changing this substance always needs energy putting in, because heating was needed once.

options.text: It stays white, because this change cannot be reversed again
options.rationale: Treats the decomposition as one-way, as most previously met reactions are.

options.text: It turns blue and the mixture warms up, as energy is released
options.rationale: The reverse of an endothermic change is exothermic, so the same amount of energy is transferred out.

options.text: It turns blue but no energy at all is transferred either way
options.rationale: Picked by students who see the colour change as physical, so expect no energy change.

mcqs.stem: A reversible reaction in a sealed flask has reached equilibrium. What is happening in the flask?

options.text: Both the forward and the reverse reactions have stopped happening
options.rationale: Reads 'nothing is changing' as 'nothing is happening'.

options.text: Equal amounts of reactants and of products are now present in it
options.rationale: Takes the everyday meaning of balance as equality of the two sides.

options.text: The forward reaction is still going but the reverse one has stopped
options.rationale: A halfway position held by students who accept that something continues but not that both do.

options.text: The forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of the point at which equilibrium is reached.

mcqs.stem: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products if equilibrium is to be reached?

options.text: A substance that escapes cannot react back, so the rates never become equal
options.rationale: Equilibrium requires the reverse reaction to match the forward one, which needs the products to stay in the apparatus.

options.text: It makes no real difference; equilibrium is reached in any container eventually
options.rationale: Treats equilibrium as something time brings about rather than something a closed system allows.

options.text: Both of the reactions stop as soon as any substance escapes from the flask
options.rationale: Combines the belief that equilibrium means stopped reactions with the idea of loss.

options.text: Escaping gas would cool the mixture down and slow both of the reactions
options.rationale: A rates-based explanation, plausible to students who explain everything through temperature.

mcqs.stem: A mixture at equilibrium in a sealed flask is left for a further hour with the conditions unchanged. What happens during that hour?

options.text: Nothing appears to change, because both of the reactions have stopped
options.rationale: The static picture of equilibrium, in which a constant appearance means a finished reaction.

options.text: Nothing appears to change, but both reactions continue at equal rates
options.rationale: Equilibrium is dynamic: the two reactions replace exactly what each other removes.

options.text: The amounts slowly become equal to each other as the mixture stands
options.rationale: Held by students who think equilibrium is reached only when the amounts are equal.

options.text: The forward reaction carries on slowly until the reactants are used up
options.rationale: Applies the one-way picture of reactions going to completion to a system already at equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: What determines the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium?

options.text: The big numbers in the balanced symbol equation
options.rationale: Transfers the use of balanced equations for calculating amounts to the equilibrium position.

options.text: Nothing, since the amounts are always equal there
options.rationale: The belief that equilibrium is by definition an equal mixture.

options.text: The conditions the reaction is carried out under
options.rationale: The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.

options.text: The order in which the substances were mixed
options.rationale: A procedural answer chosen by students with no model of what sets the position of equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: A system at equilibrium has one of its conditions changed. How does the system respond?

options.text: It cancels the change so that nothing is different at all
options.rationale: Reads 'counteract' as 'undo completely' rather than 'oppose'.

options.text: It stops reacting until the original conditions come back
options.rationale: Rests on the idea that a disturbed equilibrium means a halted reaction.

options.text: It shifts in the direction that increases the change made
options.rationale: The exact reverse of the principle, chosen when the direction of the response is guessed.

options.text: It shifts in the direction that counteracts the change made
options.rationale: The specification states that the system responds to counteract the change.

mcqs.stem: Le Chatelier’s Principle is used to make predictions about systems at equilibrium. What does it allow you to predict?

options.text: Which way the position of equilibrium moves when a condition is changed
options.rationale: The principle predicts the effects of changing conditions on the relative amounts present at equilibrium.

options.text: How much faster a reaction goes when one of the conditions is changed
options.rationale: Confuses the position of equilibrium with the rate, because rates work comes immediately before this topic.

options.text: How long a reversible reaction takes to reach equilibrium in the first place
options.rationale: The same rate-and-yield confusion, expressed as a prediction about time.

options.text: Exactly what mass of each product will be present once equilibrium is reached
options.rationale: Expects a quantitative answer, where only qualitative predictions are required.

mcqs.stem: In the equilibrium 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 the forward reaction is exothermic. The mixture is cooled. Using Le Chatelier’s Principle, what is the effect?

options.text: The equilibrium shifts towards NO2, so more NO2 is present
options.rationale: Pairs cooling with the endothermic direction instead of asking which change opposes the cooling.

options.text: The equilibrium shifts towards N2O4, so more N2O4 is present
options.rationale: Cooling is counteracted by the direction that releases energy, which here is the forward reaction.

options.text: The reaction slows down but the amounts present stay the same
options.rationale: Applies temperature to the rate only, leaving the position of equilibrium untouched.

options.text: The equilibrium shifts towards N2O4 only if pressure is raised
options.rationale: Adds a condition that was not changed, chosen by students unsure that cooling alone can shift it.

mcqs.stem: Extra A is added to a system at equilibrium: A + B ⇌ C + D. Which concentrations change before equilibrium is reached again?

options.text: Only the concentration of A changes, because A was added
options.rationale: Treats the four substances as separate stores rather than one linked system.

options.text: Only the concentrations of C and D change, and not A and B
options.rationale: Recognises that products respond but forgets that B is used up as they form.

options.text: The concentrations of all four of the substances change
options.rationale: The system is no longer at equilibrium, so the concentrations of all the substances change until it is reached again.

options.text: No concentrations change, as the system is at equilibrium
options.rationale: Assumes equilibrium is a fixed, finished state that a change cannot disturb.

mcqs.stem: In the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D, the concentration of B is increased. What happens next?

options.text: More A and B are formed, as that side has more in it now
options.rationale: Reads 'shifts towards' as moving to the side the extra substance was added to.

options.text: The extra B is used up entirely and nothing else changes
options.rationale: Assumes the system undoes the change completely, restoring the original position.

options.text: Both reactions speed up but the amounts present are the same
options.rationale: Explains the change through rate alone, leaving the equilibrium position unaltered.

options.text: More C and D are formed until equilibrium is reached again
options.rationale: If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.

mcqs.stem: Product C is continuously removed from the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D. What is the effect on the system?

options.text: More A and B react together, so more C and D are formed
options.rationale: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.

options.text: The reaction stops, because C is needed for it to continue
options.rationale: Treats the product as something the system needs in order to keep going.

options.text: The equilibrium moves towards A and B, so less C is made
options.rationale: Applies 'shift away from where the change was made' in the wrong direction.

options.text: The amount of D falls as well, to match the fall in C
options.rationale: Assumes the two products must always rise and fall together.

mcqs.stem: For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI at equilibrium, extra H2 is added. When equilibrium is reached again, the concentration of HI is higher and that of I2 is lower. What does this show?

options.text: Increasing a reactant caused more reactant to be formed
options.rationale: The wrong direction of shift, held despite the data showing HI increasing.

options.text: Increasing a reactant caused more product to be formed
options.rationale: The data show HI rising and I2 falling, which is the forward reaction running further.

options.text: Adding H2 changed the concentration of H2 and nothing else
options.rationale: Contradicted by the data, but chosen by students who expect changes to stay local.

options.text: Adding H2 must have raised the temperature of the flask
options.rationale: Reaches for a temperature explanation rather than reading the concentration data given.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 is endothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased. What happens to the amount of NO2?

options.text: It decreases, because a temperature rise favours the exothermic reaction
options.rationale: Pairs heating with 'exothermic' because both words involve heat.

options.text: It stays the same, because temperature changes only affect the rates
options.rationale: Restricts the effect of temperature to how fast equilibrium is reached.

options.text: It increases, because a temperature rise favours the endothermic reaction
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction when temperature is raised.

options.text: It increases at first and then returns to its original value again
options.rationale: Assumes the system counteracts the change completely and ends where it began.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 is exothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased. What happens to the relative amount of SO3?

options.text: It increases, because a higher temperature always gives more product
options.rationale: Carries the rates rule, that heating makes reactions go further, into equilibrium.

options.text: It increases, because heating favours the exothermic forward change
options.rationale: Links heating to the exothermic direction rather than to the one that opposes it.

options.text: It stays the same, because both sides of the equation contain oxygen
options.rationale: Reaches for the equation when the energy change is what decides the answer.

options.text: It decreases, because the endothermic reverse reaction is favoured
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an exothermic reaction when temperature is raised.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of H2 + CO2 ⇌ CO + H2O is endothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is decreased. What happens to the amount of CO?

options.text: It decreases, because cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction when temperature is lowered.

options.text: It increases, because cooling favours the endothermic forward reaction
options.rationale: Pairs cooling with 'endothermic', instead of choosing the direction that opposes cooling.

options.text: It stays the same, because cooling only slows the two reactions down
options.rationale: Treats temperature as acting on rate alone and not on the equilibrium position.

options.text: It decreases, because cooling stops the forward reaction completely
options.rationale: Right direction, wrong reason: the forward reaction continues, just less far.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 is exothermic. The flask is placed in iced water. What happens to the relative amount of N2O4?

options.text: It decreases, because cooling favours the endothermic reverse reaction
options.rationale: Matches the word 'cooling' to the word 'endothermic' rather than reasoning from counteraction.

options.text: It increases, because cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an exothermic reaction when temperature is lowered.

options.text: It decreases, because cooling always reduces the yield of a product
options.rationale: Assumes yield always follows temperature in the same direction, as rate does.

options.text: It increases, but only if the flask is squeezed to a smaller volume
options.rationale: Brings in a pressure change that was not made, chosen when cooling alone seems insufficient.

mcqs.stem: The percentage yield of product Z at equilibrium is 68% at 200 °C, 45% at 300 °C and 27% at 400 °C. What does this show about the forward reaction?

options.text: It is endothermic, since raising the temperature lowers the yield
options.rationale: Correct reading of the data with the two energy terms the wrong way round.

options.text: It is exothermic, since raising the temperature speeds it up more
options.rationale: Right conclusion from the wrong reasoning: the data are about yield, not rate.

options.text: It is exothermic, since raising the temperature lowers the yield
options.rationale: A falling yield with rising temperature is what the specification states happens for an exothermic reaction.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded without knowing the pressure that was used
options.rationale: Over-cautious answer from students who do not trust a single-variable data set.

mcqs.stem: In the gaseous equilibrium N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?

options.text: Towards N2 and H2, the side with the larger number of them
options.rationale: Associates high pressure with more gas molecules, so shifts towards that side.

options.text: Neither way, as the number of atoms is the same on each side
options.rationale: Counts atoms, which are always equal in a balanced equation, instead of molecules.

options.text: Towards NH3, but only if the temperature is raised as well
options.rationale: Adds a second condition, chosen by students unsure that pressure alone shifts the position.

options.text: Towards NH3, the side with the smaller number of molecules
options.rationale: An increase in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules.

mcqs.stem: In the gaseous equilibrium N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 the pressure is decreased. What is the effect on the equilibrium position?

options.text: It shifts towards NO2, the side with the larger number of molecules
options.rationale: A decrease in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the larger number of molecules.

options.text: It shifts towards N2O4, the side with the smaller number of molecules
options.rationale: Reverses the rule by linking low pressure to the side with fewer gas molecules.

options.text: It does not shift, but the yield of NO2 falls as the pressure falls
options.rationale: Holds that yield always follows pressure, whatever the equation shows.

options.text: It shifts towards NO2, but only if the mixture is also heated up
options.rationale: Correct direction spoiled by an extra condition that was not part of the change.

mcqs.stem: All the substances in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI are gases. The yield of HI at equilibrium is the same at 1 atm, 10 atm and 50 atm. Why does pressure have no effect here?

options.text: Raising the pressure should raise the yield, so the data are wrong
options.rationale: Trusts the rule that pressure always improves yield in preference to the data.

options.text: The symbol equation shows two molecules on each side of it
options.rationale: With equal numbers of molecules on both sides there is no side with fewer molecules to shift towards.

options.text: The equation has the same number of atoms on each side of it
options.rationale: Counts atoms rather than molecules; atoms always balance, so this cannot be the reason.

options.text: Hydrogen and iodine are both made of molecules containing two atoms
options.rationale: Notices a real feature of the formulae that has nothing to do with the pressure rule.
